title: Wanna Work Together?
speaker: Creative Commons narrator (not named)
intro: A short animated film about copyright and how Creative Commons licences let creators decide how other people may use their work.
summary: The film starts by showing how people such as teachers, artists and writers learn from and build on the work of others. It explains that when you create a photo, a song, a drawing, a film or a story, you get copyright automatically, so other people normally need your permission to use it, apart from cases of fair use. For creators who want their work to travel freely, full copyright can be too strict. Creative Commons offers free licences: on its website a creator answers a few questions, for example whether others may use the work commercially or change it, and gets a licence in about a minute. Creators keep their copyright, millions of works are now free to share and remix, and the film invites viewers to join this shared culture.

listen.q: Write what you heard about copyright: how creators get it and what it means for other people.
listen.hint: How do you get it? What do others need? What is the exception?
listen.model: Creators get copyright automatically when they make something, such as a photo or a song. Other people need the creator's permission to use the work, except in cases of fair use.

listen.q: Write what you heard about how a creator chooses a Creative Commons licence.
listen.hint: How long does it take, and what do they decide?
listen.model: On the Creative Commons website a creator answers a few questions in about a minute, for example whether other people can use the work commercially and whether they can change it.

listen.q: Write what you heard about how much shared work exists now and what the film asks viewers to do.

syn.title: Summarise with synonyms
syn.prompt: Write your own summary of the video in 70–120 words. Replace every underlined word with a synonym.
syn.text: Creative Commons [helps] creators [keep] their copyright but change its [rules]. Choosing a licence is [quick], and it [tells] the public what they are [allowed] to do.
syn.model: The film explains that anyone who makes a photo, a song or a story owns the copyright automatically, so other people normally need permission to use it. For creators who want their work to travel widely, that can be too strict. Creative Commons assists them: they retain their copyright but set new terms. The process is fast, because on the website they answer a few questions, for example about commercial use and changes. The licence then informs the public what they are permitted to do. Today millions of works can be reused and remixed for free.

adv.title: Use three adverbs
adv.prompt: Summarise the video in 60–100 words. Use all three adverbs below.
adv.model: The film explains that creators automatically own the copyright to their photos, songs and stories, so other people usually need permission to use them. However, some creators want their work to be used freely. Creative Commons gives them free licences, and choosing one takes about a minute: they decide whether others may use the work commercially or change it. Ultimately, the aim is a richer shared culture where millions of works can be reused and remixed.

rep.title: Formal account in reported speech
rep.prompt: Imagine you are writing a short report for your manager. Give a formal account of what the narrator said, in reported speech (80–120 words). Use at least two different reporting verbs and no contractions.
rep.model: The narrator explained that people who created photographs, songs or stories received copyright automatically. The narrator pointed out that other people therefore needed permission to use those works, except in cases of fair use. The narrator argued that full copyright could be too restrictive for creators who wanted their work to be shared. The narrator also stated that Creative Commons offered free licences and that a creator could choose one on its website in about a minute by deciding whether commercial use and changes were allowed. The narrator added that creators kept their copyright. Finally, the narrator concluded that millions of works could now be reused and invited viewers to join the commons.
